title: The Story of Starvation Heights
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile Linda Hazard (Linda Burfield Perry Hazard), a self-described fasting specialist with no medical degree whose fasting cure at Wilderness Heights near Alala Woods (Olalla), Washington, led to starvation deaths of patients, including sisters Claire and Dora Williamson. Covers her early life, her husband Samuel Hazard's bigamy conviction, the Williamson sisters' treatment, Claire's death, Margaret Conway's and John Herbert's intervention, Hazard's 1912 manslaughter trial and sentence, her prison term at Walla Walla, pardon, move to New Zealand, and her own death from fasting in 1938. The episode also includes a discussion of alternative medicine in the era before the Flexner Report, and a listener mail segment about cider gum trees and bush tucker. Much of the opening and mid-episode banter is off-topic.

entities.name: Fasting for the Cure of Disease

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-kilter banter about feeling weird and introduce the topic of a quack.

segments.title: Introducing Linda Hazard
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Linda Burfield Perry Hazard, a self-described fasting specialist with no medical degree, and place her within the sanitarium era and the lack of US medical regulation at the time.

segments.title: Hazard's early life and fasting method
segments.summary: Hazard was born in Minnesota in 1867, was made ill by mercury blue mass pills as a child, and was influenced by fasting doctor Edward Dewey. Her method combined intense fasting, enemas and forceful massage.

segments.title: Marriages and Minneapolis practice
segments.summary: Hazard married Edwin Perry, then Samuel Hazard, who was jailed for bigamy. The couple moved to Seattle and promoted Wilderness Heights as a cure-all.

segments.title: The Williamson sisters
segments.summary: Claire and Dora Williamson, orphaned English heiresses who were interested in natural health, were drawn to Hazard after an advertisement; they were staying at the Empress Hotel in Victoria in 1910.

segments.title: Alternative medicine before regulation
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how alternative medicine was still legal before the Flexner Report, and the ancient roots of fasting and the idea that undigested food causes disease.

segments.title: Early deaths and Gertrude Young
segments.summary: Hazard's first known patient death was Gertrude Young in 1902 at the Minneapolis practice; the coroner's autopsy found starvation rather than the paralysis Hazard cited.

segments.title: Washington practice and local support
segments.summary: Hazard began treating patients in Washington in 1907, attracting state legislators and wealthy clients, and had local support. Seven patients had died by 1911, and she performed the autopsies herself and took patients' estates.

segments.title: Sisters arrive and are starved
segments.summary: Hazard took the Williamson sisters to Seattle rather than the unfinished Alala Woods retreat, put them on a broth-only fast and massage, and they later arrived on stretchers at Wilderness Heights.

segments.title: Off-topic banter
segments.summary: Hosts digress into a tangent about TV reboots and Malcolm in the Middle, not related to the subject.

segments.title: Claire's death and Margaret Conway
segments.summary: Claire died seventeen days after arriving at the compound, weighing under fifty pounds. Governess Margaret Conway came from Australia, was denied access to Dora, and was told Dora owed a medical bill.

segments.title: Uncle John Herbert and Dora's release
segments.summary: John Herbert, the sisters' uncle, got involved through Conway, with help from the British vice consul in Tacoma. The guardianship was overturned and the bill was reduced, and Dora was released; other victims were found.

segments.title: Arrest and public reaction
segments.summary: Hazard was arrested for first-degree murder and fraud, with international press calling her the Starvation Doctor. Locals supported her and the Kitsap County prosecutor had to push the case.

segments.title: 1912 trial
segments.summary: The trial opened January 15, 1912, with about 100 prosecution witnesses. Dora testified about Claire's last moments. Hazard's defense claimed starvation could not kill, citing her book. The jury convicted her of manslaughter.

segments.title: Prison, pardon and New Zealand
segments.summary: Hazard was sentenced to two to twenty years at Walla Walla, appealed up to the US Supreme Court, and continued practicing. She knitted ponchos in prison, was pardoned, and moved to New Zealand where she drew patients. Dora returned to England and lived until 1945.

segments.title: Hazard's death and sources
segments.summary: Hazard died June 24, 1938 from self-administered fasting. The hosts recommend the 1997 book Starvation Heights by Greg Olsen.

segments.title: Listener mail: cider gum and bush tucker
segments.summary: Listener Daniel writes about the Tasmanian cider gum tree and its sap, fermented by the Palawa people, and asks for an episode on bush tucker.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to send email to Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com, and the closing credits run.
